newsitem.title: USA: NY Silver wants rent rules extended, Bruno says no.
newsitem.headline: NY Silver wants rent rules extended, Bruno says no.

text.p: New York State Assembly Democrats showed no sign of backing down in their battle over rent rules, with the Speaker proposing the system be extended 30 days, a step immediately ruled out by the Senate.
The present rent regulations, which mainly affect New York City, expire at midnight on Sunday.

Talks on the issue, which has held up a state budget, a new welfare plan, and a host of other issues, resumed at midmorning between Gov George Pataki, the Assembly Speaker, and the Senate Majority Leader, after a two-day break.

Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, who leads the Assembly Democrats, did not reveal any new willingness to compromise on the most important issue holding up an accord--vacancy decontrol, when he spoke to reporters before the leaders' meeting.

Under vacancy decontrol, a policy pushed by both the Republican governor and the Republican leader of the Senate, the state's approximately 1.2 million apartments would be returned to the free-market system once a tenant moved out or died. Landlords who tried to drive tenants out, which was a problem when vacancy decontrol was used from 1971 to 1974, would face new civil and criminal penalties.
"I think it's important to move at the table to a system that does not include vacancy decontrol," Silver said.

Promising to bring a bill to the Assembly floor on Sunday evening, when the legislature was expected to be in session, Silver and the Assembly Housing Committee Chairman proposed a moratorium on evictions from rent-regulated housing until a new bill was enacted. They also want the present system extended until July 15.

While saying he was hopeful a deal could be reached by Sunday, Silver continued to bash the governor for giving more weight to the views of landlords, who were big campaign contributors for Republicans, than to the concerns of downstate communities, that have most of the regulated apartments.

"To people living in their homes, one thing is clear: the governor's plan is unacceptable to them, the governor's plan throws them out of their houses. If it's not now, it's shortly in the future," said Silver. The Assembly and tenant advocates say vacancy decontrol would lead to the elimination of the system.

Silver said the Assembly's bill would seek to use a technique that has solved controversial issues in the past. He proposed that a joint Assembly-Senate conference committee resolve differences between the two houses' bills--assuming the Senate Republicans were to approve a measure that would be substantially similar to the Assembly Democrats' bill.

There appeared little likelihood of the Senate Republicans approving a similar measure, however. Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, stood by his plan, which he has modified to more closely ressemble the one put forward by the governor.

"There is no avoiding the fact that vacancy decontrol will protect every tenant and not force anyone to leave their apartments," Bruno said, in prepared remarks, adding there still was time to reach an accord.
He vowed: "There will be no extensions. Not for one hour. Not for one day."

The New York Times, in its Friday edition, said that behind closed doors negotiators had shown more flexibility, with Democrats floating ideas about ways to let landlords get some increases for vacant apartments, but not as much as they would get if the apartments returned to the open market.

Republicans also have proposed a number of partial vacancy decontrol ideas, the paper said, saying they ranged from only applying the policy to small apartment buildings or high-priced apartments, to gradually letting rents rise to to market-rates.

Asked about vacancy bonuses, Silver told reporters: "I would suggest to you that the governor's own words Tuesday, that everything but vacancy can find immediate ground, and that's what this debate is all about--the end of the system."
